title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is training a generative AI system on copyrighted recordings without authorization. Udio's music generation model was built using existing songs, and the resulting system could produce output similar to those works. This is a training-data problem, meaning the issue was baked in before the product reached users, not something that emerged from a particular interaction or edge case.

The dispute spread across multiple rights-holders and affected independent artists as well as major labels, indicating the scope of unlicensed material involved was large. Sony alleged over 30,000 recordings were used without permission. UMG and Warner Music each reached settlements and moved toward licensing arrangements, while Sony filed a separate lawsuit and a class action by independent artists was allowed to proceed. The scale of litigation across these distinct parties shows that no licensing review was conducted before training began, or that such a review did not result in the necessary agreements.

What is not established is whether any court has found Udio liable for copyright infringement, and the financial terms of the settlements are not public. Allegations in active lawsuits are claims, not findings, and the outcome of the Sony litigation and the independent artists' class action remains undetermined.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to end disputes over copyright infringement. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, claiming the company created music similar to existing hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission or compensation. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs while compensating artists.

This represents Udio's first major licensing deal with a major music label and marks a shift toward cooperation between the AI industry and music companies. Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since its launch. The company declined to disclose financial terms of the settlement. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, signaling growing acceptance of AI technology within the music industry.
